title_en: AI Is Upending the Lives of People Who Do Social Media Professionally
title_zh: AI 正在颠覆职业社交媒体从业者的生活：对话 Taylor Lorenz（UserMag）与 Rachel Carton（Link in Bio）
subtitle_zh: 两位社交媒体专家剖析 AI 如何重塑内容创作、营销团队与平台格局。
description: AI Is Upending the Lives of People Who Do Social Media Professionally

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios. Podcasts.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。播客。

turns.en: Radio. News.
turns.zh: 电台。新闻。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to another episode of the Odd Thoughts Podcast.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots 播客。

turns.en: I'm Tracy Alloway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: And I'm Joe Weisenthal. So we're here in Hollywood, our first ever live Odd Thoughts show in LA. And when we come to LA, I feel like we have to talk about the influencer economy, right?
turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。我们现在人在 Hollywood，这是我们 Odd Lots 第一次在 LA 做现场节目。每次来 LA，我都觉得我们必须聊聊网红经济（influencer economy），对吧？

turns.en: The influencer economy, the creator economy, people who have 8 million followers on Instagram that none of us have ever heard of. well, there's so much I don't know about this world. There's so much I need to learn. And of course, we need to learn how AI is upending all of it.
turns.zh: 网红经济、创作者经济（creator economy），那些在 Instagram 上有 800 万粉丝、可我们一个都没听说过的人。说实话，这个世界我有太多不懂的东西，有太多要学的。当然，我们还得搞清楚 AI 是怎么把这一切都掀翻的。

turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: So this is the existential question facing creators. What happens to them when creating content essentially becomes free or extremely low cost? So we have two very special guests for you. We are going to be speaking with Taylor Lorenz. She is, of course, the founder of UserMag, as well as Rachel Carton. She is a social media consultant and author also. of the Substack link in bio.
turns.zh: 所以这正是创作者面临的生存性问题（existential question）：当创作内容基本上变成免费的、或者成本极低的时候，他们会怎么样？今天我们请到了两位非常特别的嘉宾。我们要对话的是 Taylor Lorenz，她当然是 UserMag 的创始人，还有 Rachel Carton，她是一位社交媒体顾问，同时也是 Substack 通讯 Link in Bio 的作者。

turns.en: Since we're here in LA and as we've alluded to in the past, we got to learn about influencers and people with 5 million followers on Instagram and how they're dealing with this moment.
turns.zh: 既然我们人在 LA，而且我们以前也提到过，那就得了解一下网红、了解那些在 Instagram 上有 500 万粉丝的人，看看他们是怎么应对当下这个时刻的。

turns.en: Yeah, so we do, in fact, have the perfect guest.
turns.zh: 是啊，所以我们确实请到了最合适的嘉宾。

turns.en: That's right. Thrilled to welcome to the stage the one and only Taylor Lorenz, founder of Usermag, as well as Rachel Carton, social media consultant, author of the great sub-stack Link and Buy.
turns.zh: 没错。让我们热烈欢迎独一无二的 Taylor Lorenz 上台，她是 UserMag 的创始人，还有 Rachel Carton，社交媒体顾问、优秀 Substack 通讯 Link in Bio 的作者。

turns.en: Hello.
turns.zh: 你们好。

turns.en: Hello.
turns.zh: 你们好。

turns.en: Thank you both so much for doing this. Thanks for having us.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你们两位来做客。谢谢你们邀请我们。

turns.en: What are you covering these days?
turns.zh: 你们最近都在报道些什么？

turns.en: How would you.
turns.zh: 你会怎么

turns.en: Describe your coverage here?
turns.zh: 形容你现在做的这些报道？

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: I write a newsletter called Lincoln Bio. Oh, yay. It's really good.
turns.zh: 我写一份叫 Link in Bio 的通讯。哦，太棒了。它真的很好。

turns.en: Everyone should subscribe.
turns.zh: 大家都该去订阅。

turns.en: Thank you. It's about working in social media.
turns.zh: 谢谢。它是讲在社交媒体行业工作的。

turns.en: It's the primary trade publication for social media teams.
turns.zh: 它是面向社交媒体团队的首要行业刊物（trade publication）。

turns.en: And I interview.
turns.zh: 我会采访

turns.en: So I have interviewed everyone from the social team who covered Artemis to Chanti Beluga.
turns.zh: 所以我采访过的人，从报道 Artemis 的社交团队，到 Chanti Beluga，什么人都有。

turns.en: I forgot about that one. Is that already?
turns.zh: 那个我都忘了。它是不是已经

turns.en: Is that still?
turns.zh: 它还在吗？

turns.en: That was like a one week thing, right?
turns.zh: 那不就是火了一个星期的事儿嘛，对吧？

turns.en: And I am a tech journalist. I write usermag.co. That's my sub stack. I write about, I kind of do a lot of roundups about like online culture, write about tech, a lot of tech policy stuff too. Yeah.
turns.zh: 然后我呢，是一名科技记者。我写 usermag.co，那是我的 Substack。我写的内容——我经常会做很多关于网络文化（online culture）的盘点，也写科技，还有很多科技政策（tech policy）方面的东西。对。

turns.en: A little bit of everything.
turns.zh: 什么都聊一点。

turns.en: So everybody subscribe to that one as well.
turns.zh: 所以那份大家也都去订阅一下。

turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: What are the vibes like right now in social media?
turns.zh: 现在社交媒体圈的氛围（vibes）怎么样？

turns.en: It's a loaded question. All right, go on.
turns.zh: 这问题可有分量了。行，你说吧。

turns.en: Backstage, Taylor showed me a video that she was impressed by.
turns.zh: 在后台的时候，Taylor 给我看了一段让她印象深刻的视频。

turns.en: No, shut up.
turns.zh: 别，别说了。

turns.en: You guys.
turns.zh: 你们知道吗。

turns.en: She was really impressed by it.
turns.zh: 她是真的被那段视频震撼到了。

turns.en: Literally, we were backstage and I haven't been on Twitter that much today. I saw one frame of this video that was the most AI-generated crap I've ever... And I was like, did you guys see a Coca-Cola truck exploded?
turns.zh: 真的，我们当时在后台，我今天没怎么上 Twitter。我看到那段视频里的一个画面，是我见过最像 AI 生成的垃圾玩意儿……我就说，你们有没有看到一辆 Coca-Cola 卡车爆炸了？

turns.en: It was a Coca-Cola truck that was exploding Coke out.
turns.zh: 那是一辆 Coca-Cola 卡车，正往外喷可乐。

turns.en: And somebody had a bucket and she was like, did you see this?
turns.zh: 然后有个人拿着一个桶，她就说，你看到这个了吗？

turns.en: I said, Taylor, please. And then the next scene is there's actually a Mentos truck next door and the guy falls in and like explodes through the sky. And I was like, oh my God, I'm becoming. And the caption was like the AI videos that your mom sends you. Oh man. And that's what I showed Rachel.
turns.zh: 我说，Taylor，拜托。然后下一个画面是，旁边其实还有一辆 Mentos 卡车，那个人掉了进去，然后就像爆炸一样冲上了天。我当时就想，我的天，我要变成……然后配的文字大概是“你妈发给你的那些 AI 视频”。哎哟。这就是我拿给 Rachel 看的那段。

turns.en: I think that like younger people might not remember the fact that for like many years, the only content on the internet was Mentos and Coca-Cola. That's like all we looked at for like a few years.
turns.zh: 我觉得年轻人可能不记得了，有那么好多年，互联网上唯一的内容就是 Mentos 和 Coca-Cola。那几年我们看的就只有这些。

turns.en: That's like really strange.
turns.zh: 那真是太奇怪了。

turns.en: No, but here's an important question. So the people that you cover, let's start with you, Rachel. The people that you talk to who are social media professionals, do they feel as if like AI is, Is we're going to like, how is it about like, are they mostly of the frame like, oh, I can do what I do? Or do they mostly see it as an augmenter? Oh, I can do much more of the job that I know how to do for years with these new tools.
turns.zh: 不，但这里有个重要的问题。你报道的那些人——我们从你开始吧，Rachel。你接触的那些社交媒体从业者，他们是不是觉得 AI 会——我们要说，他们是怎么看的，他们是大多觉得“哦，我还是能干我这一行”，还是大多把它当成一种增强工具（augmenter），“哦，有了这些新工具，我能把我干了这么多年、驾轻就熟的工作做得更多”？

turns.en: So I think the way that AI is showing up for a lot of marketing teams is through their boss.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，对很多营销团队来说，AI 是通过他们的老板出现的。

turns.en: I wrote an article about this called Does Your Boss Have AI Brain?
turns.zh: 我为此写过一篇文章，叫《你的老板得了 AI 脑吗？》（Does Your Boss Have AI Brain?）。

turns.en: And I talked to like a hundred marketers who are dealing with an issue where their boss is asking them to use AI and their boss is using AI themselves and they're outsourcing all of their gut instincts to AI. And so I heard stories of a social manager who worked hard on a funny meme and they'll send it to their boss and they run it through Claude and ask, is this funny?
turns.zh: 我采访了大概一百个营销人，他们都在面对这样一个问题：老板要求他们用 AI，老板自己也在用 AI，还把他们所有的直觉判断都外包给了 AI。所以我听到这样的故事：一个社媒经理辛辛苦苦做了个好玩的梗图（meme），发给老板，老板把它丢进 Claude 里问一句“这个好笑吗？”

turns.en: That's so grim. That's so grim.
turns.zh: 太让人窒息了。真是太让人窒息了。

turns.en: I heard another example of a marketer who their boss only buys into ideas that came from Copilot. And so they actually will mock up their ideas into the Copilot UI to send their boss to get it approved. And so the quote that sticks with me from that article is demoralizing as hell. And so that's the way that a lot of marketers are interacting with AI is their boss sort of forcing.
turns.zh: 我还听到另一个例子，有个营销人，他老板只认可那些出自 Copilot 的点子。所以他们真的会把自己的想法做成 Copilot 界面的样子，再发给老板，好让它获得批准。那篇文章里让我印象最深的一句话是“这真是让人士气低落到极点”（demoralizing as hell）。所以很多营销人跟 AI 打交道的方式，就是被老板某种程度强行

turns.en: It upon them.
turns.zh: 强加给他们。

turns.en: And my takeaway from that wasn't like ban AI from marketing teams, but I felt like, you know, the way that AI is being implemented is sort of a free for all. And I was thinking back to my time when I worked at Condé Nast, you know, I think they had Asana onboarded and we spent months, right? Like learning how to use Asana, what's the right way to use this workflow, and that training isn't happening on marketing teams, and so it feels like there's no philosophies or guardrails for marketers to feel like their boss is giving to them.
turns.zh: 而我从中得到的结论，并不是要把 AI 从营销团队里禁掉，而是我觉得，AI 被落地的方式基本是一片毫无章法的混战。我回想起我在 Condé Nast 工作的那段时间，我记得他们上线了 Asana，我们花了好几个月，对吧？去学怎么用 Asana、用这套工作流的正确方式是什么。而这种培训在营销团队里并没有发生，所以感觉既没有理念、也没有护栏（guardrails），营销人只能觉得这是老板硬塞给他们的东西。

turns.en: Devil's advocate question.
turns.zh: 我来唱个反调（Devil's advocate）。

turns.en: I know we're talking about how grim it is to work for a boss with AI psychosis, and everyone at the moment seems to hate AI-generated content. but you could imagine a world in three to five years, maybe even sooner, where we don't, yeah, three months, where we don't actually care anymore. Like, why should we dislike AI-generated social media or marketing content?
turns.zh: 我知道我们在说，给一个得了 AI 精神错乱（AI psychosis）的老板打工有多让人窒息，而且此刻每个人似乎都讨厌 AI 生成的内容。但你可以想象一个三到五年后、甚至可能更快——对，三个月后——的世界，在那个世界里我们其实已经不在乎了。就是说，我们凭什么要讨厌 AI 生成的社交媒体或营销内容呢？

turns.en: Well, I think I can speak to it from the brand side, and I do feel like consumers have an expectation that a brand is putting creative effort into things, and the effort that they put into their social media is a reflection of the effort that they are putting into their product. And I think that consumers feel that through it. And that has always been true about creative, you know, brands like Nike have, you know, built so much of their world around their, you know, investment into creative. And so it's seen as a shortcut and it might make you ask, you know, if, your favorite Chipotle, whatever, your favorite fast food chain is using AI generated imagery. What other shortcuts might they be taking in their process? Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得我可以从品牌的角度谈谈。我确实觉得，消费者会期望一个品牌在创意上投入心思，而品牌在社交媒体上投入的心思，正反映了他们在产品上投入的心思。我觉得消费者是能透过它感受到这一点的。而这对创意来说从来都是如此，你知道，像 Nike 这样的品牌，就是围绕他们对创意的投入构建起了自己的整个世界。所以这（用 AI）会被看成走了捷径，而且它可能会让你去想，如果你最爱的那家 Chipotle、随便什么、你最爱的那家快餐连锁都在用 AI 生成的图像，那他们在流程里还可能走了哪些别的捷径？对。

turns.en: I totally agree. I think from a content standpoint too, people actually do enjoy AI generated content.
turns.zh: 我完全同意。我觉得从内容的角度来说也一样，人们其实是喜欢 AI 生成的内容的。

turns.en: It's so crazy on YouTube.
turns.zh: 在 YouTube 上这太疯狂了。

turns.en: I don't know if you guys have noticed, but All these YouTubers are just reading AI-generated scripts now, and it's so... And you look at the comments, people will be like, amazing analysis, great script. So I think people actually like it sometimes when they don't know they're consuming it. Sometimes they actively know they're consuming it. I think people just don't want to feel tricked. That's when it starts to feel bad because you're like, oh. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我不知道你们有没有注意到，现在所有这些 YouTuber 就只是在念 AI 生成的脚本，而且这实在是太……你去看评论区，大家会说“分析得太棒了，脚本写得好”。所以我觉得，有时候人们在不知道自己消费的是 AI 内容时，其实是喜欢它的。有时候他们明知是 AI 内容也照看不误。我觉得人们只是不想有被骗的感觉。那才是让人感觉糟糕的时候，因为你会想，哦。对。

turns.en: I think it was your newsletter that I first heard about the, what is it, the fruit slop or the fruit soap.
turns.zh: 我记得就是在你的通讯里，我第一次听说那个，叫什么来着，水果烂片（fruit slop）还是水果肥皂剧（fruit soap）来着。

turns.en: Et cetera. Yeah.
turns.zh: 诸如此类的。对。

turns.en: And I think you made the point you can have a bunch of people in a comment section like, oh, I'm so disappointed. Oh, you used AI for this. It's disgusting. And then they scroll to the next reel. It's like, oh, I love this story about an orange falling in love with a carrot.
turns.zh: 我觉得你提出的观点是，评论区里可以有一大帮人在那儿说“哦，我太失望了。哦，你居然用 AI 做这个。真恶心。”然后他们往下一刷，看到下一个 reel，就变成“哦，我好爱这个橙子爱上一根胡萝卜的故事”。

turns.en: Fruit Love Island. Yeah, Fruit Love Island. Fruit Love Island.
turns.zh: 水果版《爱情岛》（Fruit Love Island）。对，水果版《爱情岛》。水果版《爱情岛》。

turns.en: What do you explain this disconnect as you see it?
turns.zh: 你会怎么解释你看到的这种反差？

turns.en: Well, I think that consumers are confused in general over what they should like online right now. And I think that Fruit Love Island feels like a low stakes. They're like it's a meme and they don't care about the craft of a meme, but they care about the craft of a company that they purchase from. Um, but, and so I think, yeah, they could be the same person who's like yelling at the company for an AI generated menu and they're sending their friend AI fruit slop.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得消费者现在整体上就很困惑，不知道自己该喜欢网上的什么东西。我觉得水果版《爱情岛》感觉是件无关紧要的小事。他们觉得那就是个梗，他们不在乎一个梗做得精不精致，但他们在乎自己购买的那家公司做得用不用心。嗯，所以我觉得，对，完全可能是同一个人，一边因为一份 AI 生成的菜单冲着某家公司大喊大叫，一边又给朋友发 AI 做的水果烂片。

turns.en: Um, I sort of asked Hayes this question earlier, but in our AI generated world, I guess. How do we feel about existing content or existing incumbents when it comes to social media? Do people who already have an audience, who already have a following, who maybe have proved authenticity in some way or that they're willing to put effort into their own work, do they become more valuable in this environment? Or is it another case of low entry costs? Anyone can come in and make content for free. And so we see a sort of further trend of, I guess, what we used to call the democratization of media.
turns.zh: 嗯，这个问题我之前好像问过你们，但在我们这个 AI 生成的世界里，我想，对于社交媒体上已有的内容、已有的老牌玩家（incumbents），我们该怎么看？那些已经有受众、已经有粉丝、也许已经用某种方式证明了自己的真实性、或者证明愿意在自己的作品上下功夫的人，在这个环境里会变得更有价值吗？还是说，这又是一个进入门槛很低的例子——任何人都能进来免费做内容——于是我们看到那种，我想就是我们过去所谓的媒体“民主化”（democratization of media）的趋势进一步加剧？

turns.en: Well, I think that like, if you think about, I think it depends on the type of content you're making. Are you making deeply parasocial content about like your life and your opinions? So many creators, the value that they, like the way that media was democratized was through how-to content. If you think of like, even just the earliest YouTube videos, it was all makeup, it was how to do this. And I actually think AI is a better authority and people will turn to AI for how to fix your dishwasher. Like it's much easier to get that. So I think those creators are going to struggle. But then there are other creators that are going to use the tools to make great content and they make content that is not easily replicable. You know, maybe it's commentary that's sort of.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得，这要看你做的是哪种内容。你做的是不是那种高度拟社会关系（parasocial）的、关于你自己生活和观点的内容？很多创作者——媒体被“民主化”的方式，其实是通过教程类（how-to）内容。你想想，哪怕就是最早期的那些 YouTube 视频，全都是化妆、全是怎么做这个那个。而我确实觉得，在“怎么修好你的洗碗机”这类问题上，AI 是个更权威的来源，人们会转向 AI 去问，那样要容易得多。所以我觉得那些创作者会很难熬。但也会有另外一些创作者，他们会用这些工具做出很棒的内容，而且他们做的内容不容易被复制。你知道，也许是那种有点……的评论

turns.en: My mom, by the way, she was very proud. She was telling me that she used ChatGPT to fix her toilet recently.
turns.zh: 顺便说一下，我妈，她可得意了。她告诉我她最近用 ChatGPT 修好了她家的马桶。

turns.en: Good for her.
turns.zh: 她真棒。

turns.en: Which was, I wouldn't have expected her to be able to do that.
turns.zh: 这我原来根本想不到她能搞定。

turns.en: Taylor is a keen observer of the online discourse. One of the, you know, maybe more online than I am somehow. I'm just curious, like, you know, in the last month, you know, a month ago, there was like a lot of people arguing about data centers. And then in the last week, there were a bunch of people arguing about models themselves as this sort of like site of controversy. Do you feel like, let's just say we're talking about AI, that like... the speed with which the public takes on a new thing is it's just like an extraordinary rapid pace. And that's like, Oh, you're still arguing about data centers. Wasn't that like a sort of, Wasn't that a July issue?
turns.zh: Taylor 是网络论战（online discourse）的敏锐观察者。你在这方面也许比我还“泡在网上”。我就很好奇，你知道，就在过去一个月里，一个月前，有一大群人在争论数据中心（data centers）。然后就在过去这一周，又有一大群人在争论模型（models）本身，把它当成某种争议焦点。你会不会觉得，我们就拿 AI 来说，公众接受一个新事物的速度，那是一种非同寻常的飞快节奏。就好像，“哦，你还在争数据中心啊。那不是……那不就是七月的事儿吗？”

turns.en: That was so July. I feel like there's, I mean, there was going to be outrage on social media. Data centers is an issue of 2026. I saw, I think it was like Morris Katz, the political consultant, actually saying like people are going to make a mistake and think it's a 2028 election cycle issue. It's actually a very 2026 election cycle issue. And probably by 2028, we will have something new to get mad about.
turns.zh: 那太七月了。我觉得，我是说，社交媒体上迟早会有众怒。数据中心是 2026 年的议题。我看到，我记得像是政治顾问 Morris Katz，他其实在说，人们会犯个错误，以为这是个 2028 年选举周期的议题。它其实是个非常 2026 年选举周期的议题。而到了 2028 年，我们大概又会有新的东西可以生气了。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.zh: 但我觉得，是啊，数据中心这场论战一直很有意思，因为那些人反对 AI 的理由，跟那些觉得 AI 会把我们全杀光的生存风险派（X-risk people）非常不同。到目前为止，这两拨人还没有真正联合起来、形成任何连贯的联盟。所以我感觉也许他们应该合流。但他们的利益诉求非常不一样。顺便说一句，我可不觉得它会把我们杀光。我们会没事的。

turns.en: I was going to ask, so.
turns.zh: 我正要问，所以

turns.en: You wrote about the idea of when we talk about rogue AI potentially killing us, getting the discourse and the language about that possibility right. Give us the sort of nutshell argument. Like, what is the distinction that we need to be making here?
turns.zh: 你写过这么一个观点：当我们谈论失控的 AI（rogue AI）有可能杀死我们时，要把关于这种可能性的论述和用词说对。给我们讲讲那个精简版的核心论点吧。就是说，我们在这里需要做出的区分是什么？

turns.en: Okay, so first of all, it's not going to kill us. It's just, like, it's actually so hard to kill all humans on Earth, like, even if we wanted to.
turns.zh: 好，首先，它不会杀死我们。这只是……事实上，要杀光地球上所有人类实在太难了，哪怕我们真想那么干。

turns.en: Well, that's a relief.
turns.zh: 好吧，那我就放心了。

turns.en: So we're probably going to be fine. I think like what I think is concerning or worth interrogating is the way that we anthropomorphize AI. And that's what I wrote about is the way that people assign agency to these products. And I think in some ways it's really great to do that because we have to describe, you know, You have to sort of describe how they work, but they're not humans. And we are talking about computer programs. And I do think that when we go to these policy debates about liability and stuff, it's really important to recognize that these are not like truly living beings.
turns.zh: 所以我们大概会没事。我觉得真正让人担忧、或者说值得深挖的，是我们把 AI 拟人化（anthropomorphize）的方式。我写的就是这个，就是人们把能动性（agency）赋予这些产品的方式。我觉得这在某种程度上其实很好，因为我们得去描述，你知道，你得去描述它们是怎么运作的，但它们不是人类。我们谈论的是计算机程序。我确实觉得，当我们进入那些关于责任归属（liability）之类的政策辩论时，很关键的一点是要认识到，这些并不是真正有生命的存在。

turns.en: I saw one of the former FTC commissioners. He's like, AI isn't going to kill us. We survived the black death and that only killed 50 percent of us. So it's like, all right. Great. That's a really big.
turns.zh: 我看到一位前 FTC 委员，他说，AI 不会杀死我们。我们连黑死病（black death）都熬过来了，而那也只杀死了我们当中的 50%。所以就是，好吧。太好了。那可真是个大……

turns.en: But also just because something kills us doesn't mean it's smarter than us. You know, like a virus can kill a lot of people. It's not smarter than us. Okay.
turns.zh: 但而且，某样东西能杀死我们，并不代表它就比我们聪明。你知道，一种病毒能杀死很多人，它可并不比我们聪明。好。

turns.en: On the question of intelligence. So like, yes, this idea, like it makes you sick to your stomach to think like, oh, you've come up with something funny. And then they're like, well, my buddy Claude doesn't think that it's funny. Do you see positive productive applications of it in the marketing world?
turns.zh: 说到智能这个问题。所以，是的，这个想法——一想到“哦，你琢磨出一个好笑的东西”，然后他们说“嗯，可我的哥们儿 Claude 不觉得它好笑”，就让人胃里一阵难受。但你现在在营销圈里，有没有看到这项技术一些有成效的用法，不管是拿来做 A/B 测试之类的，就是说，好吧，嘲笑它很容易，但 AI 模型往往确实能给出相当不错的答案。你在营销世界里看到它有什么积极、有成效的应用吗？

turns.en: The, the, interesting way that I've seen it is that a lot of agencies will be selling through ideas that they want to do in the real world and in their decks or in a way to help a boss who has maybe a lack of imagination visualize what that big idea is. So I have been interested by using AI to mock something up to then be able to make it in the real world and have like a human impact on it. But so that's, that's something that I'm interested in.

turns.zh: 那它为什么吸引她？

turns.en: And, I recently published a hot takes newsletter, and I said that Threads is the most toxic social media platform. Oh, is it?
turns.zh: 而且，我最近发了一期“暴论”（hot takes）通讯，我在里面说，Threads 是最有毒（toxic）的社交媒体平台。哦，是吗？

turns.en: It is by far.
turns.zh: 它绝对是。

turns.en: Say why. Say why. Well, the way that the algorithm works, it really prioritizes replies. And so you'll get sort of dropped off into somebody's really angry reply to something. And that's what fuels it, essentially. And it turns into a very quick sort of groupthink thing. pile on in a way that is surprising.
turns.zh: 说说为什么。说说为什么。嗯，这个算法运作的方式，它真的很偏重回复（replies）。所以你会被猛地丢进某个人对某件事特别愤怒的回复里。而这基本上就是给它添柴火的东西。然后它会很快演变成一种非常迅速的群体思维（groupthink），一种以令人吃惊的方式抱团围攻（pile on）。

turns.en: Even worse than Twitter.
turns.zh: 比 Twitter 还糟。

turns.en: Twitter is like a wonderful fairyland compared to Threads.
turns.zh: 跟 Threads 比起来，Twitter 就像是一个美妙的仙境（fairyland）。

turns.en: Are you serious?
turns.zh: 你认真的吗？

turns.en: It's insane.
turns.zh: 太离谱了。

turns.en: It also does the AI-generated, we were literally just talking about this, but Threads does the AI-generated news summaries, but it's just lying. It just makes things up. She was showing me a crazy brand drama on there, but it's a crazy place.
turns.zh: 它还搞那个 AI 生成的东西——我们刚刚才在说这个——Threads 会做 AI 生成的新闻摘要，但它就是在撒谎。它就是瞎编。她刚才还给我看了一出在那上面的疯狂品牌大战（brand drama），反正那就是个疯狂的地方。

turns.en: We only have a few minutes left, so I'm going to ask a question that we sort of alluded to at the beginning. But I'm sure there are a lot of people out in the audience who would like to grow their social media accounts and their presence. But what are your top tips in the age of AI for getting to, as Joe says, an account that mysteriously has 5 million followers?
turns.zh: 我们只剩几分钟了，所以我要问一个我们在开头就暗示过的问题。但我相信台下有很多观众，是想把自己的社交媒体账号和影响力做起来的。那么在 AI 时代，你们对于如何做到——用 Joe 的话说——一个莫名其妙就有 500 万粉丝的账号，有什么顶级建议？

turns.en: What are yours? I would say the accounts that I see that are growing right now, all their content has a real like through line of familiarity. It's like they're creating their own TV show. There's a cook at a restaurant who wears meta glasses and just records what he's cooking. I believe he's grown to like 500,000 followers in maybe two or three months, like Gil Holy Cooks. And so that's all that they post is just like my show is on. They are making an episode every day. Yeah, it seems to be a lot of like serialized content. It's all becoming shows. You have to really think about entertaining. I think the era of like sharing your life is like very declining.
turns.zh: 你有什么建议？我会说，我现在看到的那些正在增长的账号，他们所有的内容都有一条真正的、贯穿始终的熟悉感（through line of familiarity）。就好像他们在创作自己的电视节目。有一个在餐厅当厨师的人，戴着 Meta 眼镜，就录他自己在做什么菜。我记得他大概两三个月就涨到了 50 万粉丝，就像 Gil Holy Cooks 那样。所以他们发的全部内容就是“我的节目开播了”。他们每天都在做一集。对，这似乎是很多连载式（serialized）的内容。一切都在变成节目。你真的得好好琢磨怎么去娱乐大家。我觉得那种“分享你的生活”的时代，正在非常迅速地衰退。

turns.en: Nobody cares. And I think like, so don't try to be a lifestyle influencer in 2026. It's not, there's a lot of anger towards those people.
turns.zh: 没人关心那个。而且我觉得，所以，别在 2026 年去试着当一个生活方式网红（lifestyle influencer）了。那不是……大家对那类人有很多的愤怒。

turns.en: I'm curious, though, speaking of the lifestyle influencers, are people signing deals with like, yes, you can use my voice. You could create a digital clone of me. You can have 10 versions of me. Like, is that happening?
turns.zh: 不过我很好奇，说到生活方式网红，有没有人在签这样的合约，就是“可以，你们可以用我的声音。你们可以给我做一个数字分身（digital clone）。你们可以有 10 个版本的我”。这种事正在发生吗？

turns.en: Yeah, I wrote a piece for Vanity Fair recently about this. And CIA has like really leaned into this. They have what's called the CIA vault where like all of their big stars, like, you know, they use AI to like. basically cut down on people. Right now, it's mostly like the influencer or the star celebrity will show up for like one day, but then they'll use it to like tweak the takes or, you know, tailor it for different audiences and different, and I do think that that is probably the way that it's going to go.
turns.zh: 对，我最近为 Vanity Fair 写了一篇关于这个的文章。CIA 真的很投入这一套。他们有所谓的“CIA 保险库”（CIA vault），他们所有的大明星，你知道，他们用 AI 来基本上削减人手。现在的情况主要是，那个网红或者那位明星名人会露面大概一天，但然后他们会用它来微调各个镜头（takes），或者你知道，针对不同的受众去做调整，不同的……而我确实觉得，那大概就是它未来会走的方向。

turns.en: I guess Bloomberg owns the rights to our.
turns.zh: 我想 Bloomberg 拥有我们

turns.en: Voices, right?
turns.zh: 声音的版权，对吧？

turns.en: We don't really license them, but.
turns.zh: 我们其实并不怎么把它们授权出去，但是。

turns.en: They're going to start generating just endless odd lots.
turns.zh: 他们要开始没完没了地生成 Odd Lots 了。

turns.en: They might do.
turns.zh: 他们可能会。

turns.en: You know, one thing I like reading about, Rachel, in your subtext, it's like, you talk about like the various tactics, right? Like carousels or what are some of the other ones that are, what's hot these days in terms of like presentation approaches?
turns.zh: 你知道，Rachel，我喜欢在你的 Substack 上读到的一件事是，你会讲到各种策略，对吧？比如轮播图（carousels），或者还有哪些别的，就是最近在呈现方式（presentation approaches）上什么是热门的？

turns.en: Well, so Instagram shared with my audience a really helpful chart that showed what each sort of, um, format is for. And so carousels and reels are for reaching a new audience. Those will go out to non-followers. And what fuels the algorithm right now is non-follower views. If it's something that only your audience understands, they're like, that's not entertaining enough.
turns.zh: 嗯，是这样，Instagram 跟我的受众分享过一张特别有用的图表，展示了每种格式（format）分别是用来干什么的。所以轮播图和 reel 是用来触达新受众的，它们会被推送给非粉丝（non-followers）。而现在给算法添动力的，正是非粉丝的观看量。如果某个东西只有你自己的受众才看得懂，他们就会觉得，那不够有娱乐性。

turns.en: We're not going to put it on the main channel.
turns.zh: 我们不会把它放到主频道上去。

turns.en: And then single image posts just are for your audience. And then stories and DMs, they see as where community happens. And there was a conversation, I think at Bloomberg Screen Time, actually, where Adam Mosseri said that the social and social media is not through sharing, you know, an image of your family anymore necessarily. It is through DMing your friends something that reminds you of them. And I thought that was very unfortunate but clarifying in terms of what it means to be social on social media anymore. And it's really connecting through DMs and sending them a meme that reminds them of them more than an important update in their life. Interesting.
turns.zh: 然后单张图片的帖子就只是给你自己的受众看的。再然后故事（stories）和私信（DM），他们把这看作社区（community）发生的地方。有一场对话，我记得其实是在 Bloomberg Screen Time 上，Adam Mosseri 说，社交媒体上的“社交”，已经不再一定是通过分享一张你家人的图片来实现了。它是通过给你朋友私信发一个能让你想起他们的东西来实现的。我觉得这一点很令人遗憾，但也把问题讲清楚了——就是说，在社交媒体上“社交”到底意味着什么。它真的更多是通过私信、给他们发一个能让他们想起自己的梗，而不是他们生活里的一条重要更新。有意思。

turns.en: Taylor and Rachel, thank you so much for joining us at Odd Lots Live, closing out the show in such a fascinating area. Really appreciate talking to both of.
turns.zh: Taylor、Rachel，非常感谢你们来到 Odd Lots Live，在这么一个引人入胜的领域为我们的节目收官。真的很感激能和你们两位聊这一场。

turns.en: You.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们。

turns.zh: 感谢收看和收听。
